questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main claim about workplace distraction?
choices: It often grows from vague expectations among stakeholders, not only from devices
It is caused only by weak willpower
It disappears if people attend more meetings

explanation.gentle: The chapter says unclear expectations often produce interruption.
explanation.direct: Stakeholder ambiguity is treated as a major source of distraction.
explanation.competitive: The pings are often running on fog, not fate.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to sync with stakeholders at work?
choices: To align expectations about availability, response windows, urgency, and escalation before interruptions multiply
To answer every message instantly so nobody gets upset
To disappear from communication whenever focus matters

explanation.gentle: The chapter is about setting expectations in advance.
explanation.direct: Syncing means explicit alignment, not instant obedience or hiding.
explanation.competitive: Mark the lanes before the traffic starts lying.

questions.prompt: Why does ambiguity create so many interruptions?
choices: Because people fill missing expectations with quick contact and guesses
Because ambiguity always improves collaboration
Because technology forces every message to be urgent

explanation.gentle: People interrupt more when they do not know the rules.
explanation.direct: Unspoken expectations become reactive contact by default.
explanation.competitive: If nobody marked the lane, everyone starts swerving.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter mention remote work and videoconferencing?
choices: Because more channels can make ambiguity travel faster and feel more urgent
Because remote work eliminates coordination problems
Because video calls should replace every other form of contact

explanation.gentle: More tools can create more pressure when norms stay unclear.
explanation.direct: Remote and video-heavy contexts multiply the speed of ambiguous requests.

questions.prompt: Which of these belongs in stakeholder syncing?
choices: Clarifying response windows and what truly counts as urgent
Letting every stakeholder define your interruptions informally
Refusing all meetings without explanation

explanation.gentle: The chapter wants timing and urgency rules to be named clearly.
explanation.direct: Expectation-setting around response and escalation is central here.
explanation.competitive: Paint the lane instead of pretending traffic will self-sort.

questions.prompt: A team treats every group-chat message like a crisis. What is the stronger diagnosis?
choices: The team never defined normal response expectations or escalation rules
The team needs more notifications
The team should avoid all collaboration

explanation.gentle: The chapter would look for missing norms first.
explanation.direct: The interruption problem is likely coordination ambiguity.
explanation.competitive: The chat is pretending to be urgent because nobody demoted it.

questions.prompt: What mistake does the chapter avoid by refusing generic etiquette language?
choices: Blaming personalities when the real issue is an unclear system
Assuming every coworker is naturally perfect
Treating work as something that needs no coordination

explanation.gentle: The chapter focuses on agreements rather than on judging people.
explanation.direct: It treats interruption as a structural default, not merely a manners problem.
explanation.competitive: Broken operating systems should not get rewritten as personality gossip.

questions.prompt: What limit does the chapter keep on stakeholder syncing?
choices: It must still respect real shared obligations and genuine urgency
It allows a person to vanish from collaboration entirely
It means every request should be delayed automatically

explanation.gentle: The chapter does not treat focus as an excuse to disappear.
explanation.direct: Expectation-setting must coexist with real responsibility.

questions.prompt: How does syncing with stakeholders support traction?
choices: It makes protected work time visible and easier for others to coordinate around
It proves that work should be done alone
It turns every channel into an urgent channel

explanation.gentle: People can work with your focus time more easily when they know the rules.
explanation.direct: Traction gets stronger when protected time is legible instead of private.
explanation.competitive: A real border gets respected more than a private wish.

questions.prompt: Why is this chapter the right bridge to asking the critical question in Chapter 11?
choices: Because aligned expectations reduce background chaos so incoming triggers can be judged more clearly
Because after syncing there are no more triggers at all
Because the next chapter is unrelated to work attention

explanation.gentle: The next chapter works better once the environment is less confusing.
explanation.direct: Expectation-setting clears coordination fog before the moment of trigger evaluation.
explanation.competitive: The critical question lands better when the ping is not backed by a swamp.
